"Bloodied but unbowed."

It’s a powerful line. William Ernest Henley wrote it in his famous poem ‘Invictus’ while surviving a grueling, painful bone disease. But there is a massive difference between a Victorian poet enduring physical agony and a Vice President using his words to dodge an impeachment trial.

Dropping a dramatic literary reference to a scrum of Senate reporters before walking away isn't courage—it’s a deflection. Henley’s poem is about mastery over one's own soul; it wasn't written to help public officials evade constitutional accountability.

You stood before the flashing lights, wrapped in the language of a martyr, and claimed to be bloodied but unbowed.

But you do not know the taste of your own blood. You only know how to bleed the nation dry.

The real bludgeoning does not happen in the air-conditioned halls of the Senate, nor does it take place under the sterile glare of a press conference you refused to face. The real bludgeoning happens in the dark, quiet corners of this country—in the empty pockets of parents who cannot afford tuition, in the hollow stomachs of children whose futures were bartered away for confidential funds, and in the exhausted spirits of commuters who build their entire lives around the failures of your governance.

For decades, your family built an empire on carefully packaged mythology. You spun narratives of strength while silences grew longer, and you demanded blind loyalty while accountability was treated as an insult. You treat our democracy like a fantasy realm where the loudest monologue wins the crown, expecting the masses to applaud the cleverness of your scripts.

But we are the ones who have been fighting fairly.

We are the ones who follow the rules, pay our taxes, line up in the heat, and respect the laws of the land, even when those laws are weaponized against us. We do not get to drop a single, dramatic catchphrase and walk away from our consequences. We have to show up, day after day, bearing the weight of your choices.

So let the record reflect who is truly unbowed.

It is not the politician running from an impeachment trial behind a wall of security guards and calculated soundbites. It is the common folk. It is the jeepney driver, the teacher, the student, the writer—the ordinary Filipino who, despite being robbed, lied to, and red-tagged, still refuses to break.

You may hold the realm for now, Inday, but your borrowed poetry belongs to us. We are the ones who are bloodied by your greed and audacity. And we are the ones who remain unbowed.

"Bloodied but unbowed."

It’s a powerful line. William Ernest Henley wrote it in his famous poem ‘Invictus’ while surviving a grueling, painful bone disease. But there is a massive difference between a Victorian poet enduring physical agony and a Vice President using his words to dodge an impeachment trial.

Dropping a dramatic literary reference to a scrum of Senate reporters before walking away isn't courage—it’s a deflection. Henley’s poem is about mastery over one's own soul; it wasn't written to help public officials evade constitutional accountability.

You stood before the flashing lights, wrapped in the language of a martyr, and claimed to be bloodied but unbowed.

But you do not know the taste of your own blood. You only know how to bleed the nation dry.

The real bludgeoning does not happen in the air-conditioned halls of the Senate, nor does it take place under the sterile glare of a press conference you refused to face. The real bludgeoning happens in the dark, quiet corners of this country—in the empty pockets of parents who cannot afford tuition, in the hollow stomachs of children whose futures were bartered away for confidential funds, and in the exhausted spirits of commuters who build their entire lives around the failures of your governance.

For decades, your family built an empire on carefully packaged mythology. You spun narratives of strength while silences grew longer, and you demanded blind loyalty while accountability was treated as an insult. You treat our democracy like a fantasy realm where the loudest monologue wins the crown, expecting the masses to applaud the cleverness of your scripts.

But we are the ones who have been fighting fairly.

We are the ones who follow the rules, pay our taxes, line up in the heat, and respect the laws of the land, even when those laws are weaponized against us. We do not get to drop a single, dramatic catchphrase and walk away from our consequences. We have to show up, day after day, bearing the weight of your choices.

So let the record reflect who is truly unbowed.

It is not the politician running from an impeachment trial behind a wall of security guards and calculated soundbites. It is the common folk. It is the jeepney driver, the teacher, the student, the writer—the ordinary Filipino who, despite being robbed, lied to, and red-tagged, still refuses to break.

You may hold the realm for now, Inday, but your borrowed poetry belongs to us. We are the ones who are bloodied by your greed and audacity. And we are the ones who remain unbowed.

Ang “hearsay” sa Tagalog ay maaaring isalin bilang:

* Sabi-sabi – impormal at pinakakaraniwang gamit.
* Tsismis – kung ang narinig ay walang matibay na ebidensya at kumakalat lamang.
* Balitang narinig lamang – mas pormal na paglalarawan.
* Salaysay batay sa narinig – karaniwang ginagamit sa legal na konteksto.

Halimbawa:

* English: That’s just hearsay.
* Tagalog: Sabi-sabi lang iyan. o Narinig lang iyan sa iba.

Sa legal na konteksto, ang hearsay ay tumutukoy sa ebidensiyang batay lamang sa sinabi ng ibang tao at hindi sa mismong personal na kaalaman ng testigo, kaya kadalasan ay hindi ito tinatanggap bilang ebidensya sa korte.

That conclusion does not necessarily follow.
If the prosecutor's repeated objections were intended to disrupt or distract the flow of the defense's cross-examination, that would not mean the defense "failed." Repeated objections can interrupt counsel's rhythm and momentum, but they do not determine the effectiveness of the cross-examination. What matters is whether the defense was able to test the witness's credibility, examine the foundation of the evidence, expose inconsistencies, and preserve legal issues for the tribunal's consideration.
Likewise, the fact that an investigation was conducted before the evidence was presented does not automatically establish that the evidence is authentic, admissible, or reliable. An investigation may gather evidence, but the party offering that evidence still bears the burden of laying the proper foundation and demonstrating its authenticity and admissibility under the applicable rules of evidence. The defense has every right to challenge that process through cross-examination.
Ultimately, the effectiveness of a cross-examination is determined by the tribunal after considering the entire record—not by the number of objections made or by the mere existence of an investigation. The burden remains on the party offering the evidence to establish its authenticity, reliability, and admissibility, and the defense is entitled to rigorously test every aspect of that evidence.
